title: How long it takes
hookLine: the full Nitnem takes an hour or more, and traditions differ slightly on which banis are included

cards: Japji, Jaap, the savaiyas, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras, Sohila. You've now met every Nitnem bani, spread from before breakfast to just before sleep.
So, the way you'd read a recipe before you start cooking: what does a full day of it actually take? And is everyone doing exactly the same thing?
Two plain questions, two plain answers, and neither is meant to scare anyone off.

teach.h: AN HOUR OR MORE A DAY.
teach.b: First, the time. The morning banis are the long part: Japji, Jaap, the savaiyas, Chaupai and all of Anand, read at a steady pace, fill most of the hour. Someone who has said them every day for years goes faster.
Rehras in the evening is shorter, and Kirtan Sohila at night takes only a few minutes. So a full Nitnem is an hour or more across the day.

Second, the differences. Sikhs share the core, but not every detail is the same everywhere. The Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht lists three morning banis; other Sikhs, especially those who have taken amrit, say five.

teach.h: A VOW FOR SOME, A ROAD FOR OTHERS.
teach.b: Some traditions, like the Damdami Taksal and some jathas, recite a longer Rehras or a longer Chaupai. Some Sikhs add more, like Sukhmani or Asa di Var in the morning.
These are differences of practice within one faith, not a ranking of who prays properly.
Third, the most useful thing. Sikhs who have taken amrit commit to Nitnem as part of their vows. For many others, and certainly for learners, it's normal to grow into it.
A child might learn the Mul Mantar first, then Japji's first pauri, then more.
An adult coming back to the faith might begin with Japji alone, or Sohila at night. Nobody arrives at the full hour on day one. Nitnem means the daily rule, and its weight is on daily.
One bani, said every day, becomes a path worn across a field.

how: A full Nitnem takes an hour or more each day; Sikhs who have taken amrit keep it as part of their vows, while many others and newcomers begin with one bani, such as Japji or Sohila, and add more over time.

games.why: many begin with one bani, like Japji or Sohila. Nitnem is a daily rule: the daily part matters more than the size.

practice: Close your eyes and, without running through a list, wait to see which bani comes back on its own: a line, a tune, a picture. Not the one you think you should pick; the one that comes back. Hold it in mind and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Bani. A single Guru's utterance, like Japji or Sohila; a full Nitnem is an hour or more a day, and many grow into it one bani at a time.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bani, the word, the Guru's utterance; each Nitnem hymn is a bani.
